newsitem.title: NORWAY: UBN 1996 net profits down 21 percent.
newsitem.headline: UBN 1996 net profits down 21 percent.

text.p: Union Bank of Norway, the country's biggest savings bank, on Thursday announced a 21 percent drop in 1996 net profits but proposed that the dividend be unchanged at 15 crowns per primary capital certificate, a hybrid share.
The profit came to 851 million crowns, down from 1.07 billion in 1995.
UBN President Kjell Kran said he was pleased with the 1996 result because there had been a good rise in volume and very favourable figures for losses and default.
After tax, and a provision of 155 million crowns for current and future reorganisation measures, the return on equity was 13.8 percent, he said in a statement.

"I expect Union Bank of Norway's 1997 financial result to be somewhat weaker," Kran said. "Excess capacity in the market will probably result in the customer spread falling also in 1997. Nor can we expect such abnormal loss figures this year.
"In spite of this, 1997 should produce a good financial result for the group," he said.
Kran said 1997 would be a very important year for the bank because many of its offices would begin to use new technology in order to serve customers better and provide more quality.

"1997 will also see further development in the cooperation we have entered into with five regional savings banks. We hope the result of this cooperation will prove to be positive, so that other savings banks will join us," he said.
Operating expenses rose to 2.98 billion from 2.65 billion while operating profit before losses came to 1.13 billion, down from 1.43 billion crowns.
Net interest income fell to 2.56 billion crowns from 2.78 billion while pre-tax operating profit dropped to 1.17 billion from 1,41 billion.
Banks are battling narrowing interest margins in Norway's overbanked financial community.
UBN said the average margin fell from 3.5 percent at the end of 1995 to 2.9 percent at the end of 1996.
"Competition in the market is growing constantly, and has resulted in the bank's margins being considerably narrower," a statement said.
But the loan volume growth continued a positive trend with a 12-month growth of 14 percent, up from 10 percent in 1995.
Corporate loans rose by 19 percent while loans to private customers increased by 10 percent.

"A substantial growth in volumes, particularly for loans to business customers, higher income from subsidiaries and net recoveries on loan losses had a positive impact on the group result," the bank said.
